fields.h1: Build a Pricing Survey That Shows What Buyers Will Pay
fields.hero_description: Build a pricing survey that tests price points, charts what buyers will pay, and saves every answer to a database you own.
fields.features_heading: What a Pricing Survey Needs to Do
fields.features_subheading: A pricing survey asks buyers what they would pay for a product and the point at which they would stop buying.
fields.feature_1:
The four price questions, in order

Asks at what price the product feels too cheap, a bargain, getting expensive, and too expensive. The survey checks each set and sends back a bargain price set above too expensive.
fields.feature_2:
Price ladders that adapt per answer

Raises the price one step when a respondent says yes and lowers it one step on a no. The ladder stops at each person's ceiling, and every step is saved as its own row for analysis.
fields.feature_3:
Curves and revenue on one dashboard

Plots the price curves, the acceptable range, and the revenue at each tested price from the response table. Charts update as answers arrive, with no spreadsheet step between.
fields.feature_4:
Answers joined to plan and segment

Pulls each customer's plan, seat count, and region from your CRM into the response. Any price chart splits by segment, showing where a price suits small teams and loses big ones.
fields.feature_5:
Reach buyers by email, page, or link

Emails the survey to current customers, opens it on your pricing page, or shares a link with a research panel. Responses are never capped, and all of them land in the same table.
fields.feature_6:
The whole survey app, exported

Exports the survey logic, the price charts, and the response database to your GitHub repository on paid plans. Run it on your own servers, or keep changing it in Emergent by prompt.

fields.tab_content_1:
The band between too cheap and too expensive

Before launching a reporting add-on, a SaaS team sends the four Van Westendorp questions to 412 trial users as a price sensitivity survey. The curves cross at $19 and $36, marking the acceptable range, and the optimal price point lands at $24. Each response is saved with the user's plan and company size.
fields.tab_content_2:
A price ladder for a meal-kit box

A meal-kit brand shows each shopper one weekly price for its family box, then a higher price after a yes and a lower one after a no. Of 600 shoppers, 420 would buy at $10 and 336 at $14. The box launches at $14, where revenue per 100 shoppers peaks at $784.
fields.tab_content_3:
Who might cancel over a $10 increase

Ahead of moving the Team plan to $59 a month, a project tool asks 1,240 current customers how the new price changes their plans. Each response carries the account's seat count and renewal date. An account that says it would cancel triggers a Slack alert to its owner, comment included. Nine did in the first week.
fields.tab_content_4:
One question when a visitor stalls on pricing

Visitors who stay on the pricing page for 40 seconds without choosing a plan see one question about what stopped them. Of 300 replies this month, 114 said too expensive for their team size, a case for a smaller tier. Anyone who picks need a quote reaches sales in HubSpot as a lead.

fields.howto_title: How to Run a Pricing Survey
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to plan a pricing survey that returns a price you can defend, then build it with Emergent.
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Match the method to the question
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Ask the people who would pay
fields.howto_step_1_des: Write down what the answers will settle, such as a launch price for a new product or an increase for current customers. Pricing surveys built around one decision get read and acted on. Note the date you need the answer, since it sets how long the survey can run.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Van Westendorp pricing survey questions suit a product with no price yet, because they return a range. A Gabor-Granger ladder suits a shortlist of prices, because it shows which one earns the most. Describe the product before either, or respondents price a guess.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Survey current customers about an increase and trial users or a screened panel about a launch. Ask for plan, team size, and role up front. One blended number can hide two different buyers, and those fields let you split the result later.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Skip the pricing survey template and write out the product, the method, the price points, and where answers go. Emergent builds the survey, its logic, and a response table with the charts. A later change, like a $29 step on the ladder, takes one more message.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Send the survey to about 20 people first. Check that their four prices rise in order and that nobody answers per year when you asked per month. Fix any confusing wording before the full send, or the curves end up mixing two different questions.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Read every segment on its own
fields.howto_step_6_des: Look at the acceptable range or the revenue peak for each segment before the total. A price that suits freelancers may lose agencies with 50 seats. Where two segments disagree by a wide margin, that gap is often the argument for a second tier.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Test the price with real buyers
fields.howto_step_7_des: Treat survey answers as stated intent, not purchases. Before committing, offer the chosen price to a share of new sign-ups for a few weeks. Compare their conversion with what the survey predicted, and adjust the price if the two disagree.

plan.angle: The top 10 is method explainers and question lists (Voxco, SurveyMonkey, Qualtrics, Attest, quantilope, Pricing Society) plus a few survey-tool pages (Survio, Usersnap). They describe Van Westendorp and Gabor-Granger in the abstract and stop at the questions. This page shows four pricing surveys running as apps: the range chart that comes out of the four price questions, a ladder that finds the revenue peak, a check with current customers before an increase that alerts the account owner, and a one-question poll on the pricing page. Every answer sits in a database the company owns, joined to plan and segment.
